Feature trajectories of dots in four conditions (A-D) in our initial experiments. Within each of the
four corrresponding figures, dot fields are distinguished by line style (dotted or solid) and dot field color is
given by line color. Within the upper plots of each figure, motion type (i.e. clockwise, counterclockwise, or
translation) is given by vertical lplacement. Similarly, within the lower plots, depth (Near vs Far) is indicated by
vertical placement. Left column (No depth swap: A and C). A) The delayed dot field is Red and Near.
The translating dots are the delayed dots and are also Red and Near. Hence Dots, Color, and Depth are all "cued".
C) The delayed dot field is Green and Far whereas the translating dots are Red and Far are of the non-delayed
dot field: hence all Dot, Color, and Depth are considered "uncued". Left column (Depth swap:B and D). B) As in A,
the delayed dot is Red, and Near. At translation onset, however, dots in the two depth planes switch.
As a result, the translating dots are still of the delayed dot field and are still red, but they no longer in the same
depth fieldas the delayed onset. Hence, Dot and Color are considered cued but Depth is uncued. D) The delayed
dot field is green and in the Far depth plane. The translating dots are of the undelayed depth field and of a
different color than the delayed dots. Thus Dot and Color are uncued. Depth due to the depth swap is cued.
The Depth Swap manipluation thus pits Dot cueing (dot identify or dot x-y position) vs. Depth cueing. Color swaps
have been found to have minimal impact and thus is not considered here.
D

Feature trajectories of dots in four conditions (A-D) of our initial experiments. Within each of the
four corrresponding figures, dot fields are distinguished by line style (dotted or solid) and dot field color is
given by line color. Within the upper plots of each figure, motion type (i.e. clockwise, counterclockwise, or
translation) is given by vertical lplacement. Similarly, within the lower plots, depth (Near vs Far) is indicated by
vertical placement. Left column (No depth swap: A and C). A) The delayed dot field is Red and Near.
The translating dots are the delayed dots and are also Red and Near. Hence Dots, Color, and Depth are all "cued".
C) The delayed dot field is Green and Far whereas the translating dots are Red and Far are of the non-delayed
dot field: hence all Dot, Color, and Depth are considered "uncued". Left column (Depth swap:B and D). B) As in A,
the delayed dot is Red, and Near. At translation onset, however, dots in the two depth planes switch.
As a result, the translating dots are still of the delayed dot field and are still red, but they no longer in the same
depth fieldas the delayed onset. Hence, Dot and Color are considered cued but Depth is uncued. D) The delayed
dot field is green and in the Far depth plane. The translating dots are of the undelayed depth field and of a
different color than the delayed dots. Thus Dot and Color are uncued. Depth due to the depth swap is cued.
The Depth Swap manipluation thus pits Dot cueing (dot identify or dot x-y position) vs. Depth cueing. Color swaps
have been found to have minimal impact and thus is not considered here.
Left (A vs C): Results for the no-depth swap conditions confirm and extend previous studies by demonstrating that a delayed dot
field enjoys a processing advantage even when dot fields are separated in depth: directional accuracy is significantly better
for the delayed dot field (blue) than for the undelayed dot field (brown). Color and depth could also considered to be cued in
this design. Right (B vs D): Results for the depth swap condition confirm that delayed dots enjoy a processing advantage.
Conversely no evidence of a depth cueing advantage was found. From these data, we tentatively conclude that position in x-y
space is important for the cueing effect, position in depth is not.
